newsitem.title: GERMANY: Kohl's policies attacked after record jobless rate.
newsitem.headline: Kohl's policies attacked after record jobless rate.

text.p: German Chancellor Helmut Kohl's economic stewardship drew fire on Sunday as a key labour leader blamed his government for the nation's record-high jobless rate and speculation mounted he may no longer be fit to govern.

Three days after Germany reported the January jobless total had climbed to 4.66 million people, the highest level since 1933, labour leaders, politicians and commentators demanded more innovative steps and fast action to solve the problem.

"The record high unemployment rate is a result of the federal government's policies," Herbert Mai, head of Germany's public sector service workers' union OeTV, told the German newspaper Express. "I miss active job creation policies," he added.

Noting that Kohl's dearest goal, preparing Germany for Europe's planned monetary union in 1999, dictates more strict spending cuts, the German newspaper Bild am Sonntag said Kohl could do little about high unemployment rates at the moment.
"Kohl is sitting in a Euro-trap," Bild said, adding that this dilemma explained the chancellor's reluctance to announce his candidacy for another term in office.

Leaders of the opposition Social Democrats were equally critical of Kohl, saying he had lost his authority and suggesting another leader, German President Roman Herzog, should help tackle labour market problems.

German newspaper Welt am Sonntag indicated dissent had even spread to the business community and said Hilmar Kopper, the chairman of Germany's largest commercial bank Deutsche Bank, had sharply criticsed the Kohl government.
Deutsche Bank spokesman Hellmut Hartmann however denied the alleged statements, saying the newspaper's front-page article was "completely false".

The newspaper wrote that Kopper, during a meeting with parliamentarians, had suggested Bonn lacked the initiative needed to create a more flexible economy and that it was impossible to halve the jobless rate by 2000.
But Hartmann, in a letter Welt am Sonntag's editor, said "How (Kopper's) praise for the ruling coalition's reform plans could be transformed into massive criticism is incomprehensible to me.".
Christian Democrat (CDU) parliamentarian Gunnar Uldall, present at the meeting with Kopper, also told Reuters that Welt am Sonntag's report "tried to give an impression that was definitely false".
Kohl backtracked on Thursday from an often ridiculed, previous stance saying it was his goal, rather than his forecast, that unemployment would be halved by 2000.
But OeTV chief Mai said: "With our current policies there will be no halving of the jobless rate."

"We do not create jobs by cutting workers' sick pay or paring back job protection measures," he added, referring to a highly controversial five month-old law which lets employers cut workers' salaries to 80 percent during illness.
Germany's opposition Social Democrats demanded fresh leadership in the battle against unemployment.

"Germany's president (Roman Herzog) clearly has greater authority than the chancellor, especially after Kohl let last year's Alliance for Jobs break down," Hans Eichel, premier of the state of Hesse, told the newspaper Bild.

Last year German employers, unions and government officials got together in an attempt to hash out new strategies to cut the jobless rate. But little progress was made and unions now say Kohl failed to keep certain promises.

Reaction to the suggestion was lukewarm, however. Herzog's spokesman Roland Lohkamp told Welt am Sonntag the president had no executive powers and that appropriate parties should live up to their responsibilities.
